lessons.title: Close-up: what the floor and the bed tell

zoom.label: The floor at the bottom of the picture: a shallow copper basin, a cloth hanging over its rim

c1.text: Level one ended with the basin. Here it is, on the floor at the bottom: a shallow copper basin, with a cloth over its rim.

zoom.label: The floor at the bottom of the picture: a shallow copper basin, a cloth hanging over its rim

c1q.text: Two scholars link this basin to what?

sources.title: Claudia Renzi, 'Caravaggio, la Morte della Vergine e una cortigiana da lui amata', About Art Online, 2025 (our translations)
Keith Christiansen, 'Low Life, High Art', The New Republic, 8 December 2010

c1a.text: A church picture, yes, but both scholars think of the body.

correction.tempting: It was painted to hang above a church altar.
correction.truth: Both scholars connect the basin with washing the dead woman's body.
correction.evidence: Renzi (2025): an allusion to washing the body. Christiansen (2010): the ritual cleansing of the body.

c1b.text: Yes. Renzi reads it as a hint at washing the body; Christiansen calls it a reminder of physical death and the ritual cleansing of the body.

c1c.text: Close, but both scholars mean the whole body.

correction.tempting: The friars of this church went barefoot.
correction.truth: Both scholars connect the basin with washing the dead woman's body, not feet.
correction.evidence: Renzi (2025): an allusion to washing the body. Christiansen (2010): the ritual cleansing of the body.

c1m.text: A basin for washing the body: that is how two scholars read it.

zoom.label: The Virgin's head at the right end of the bed, eyes closed, her left hand hanging down

c2.text: Level one: the church took this Mary down. Now zoom to her head, at the right end of the bed, and look just around it.

zoom.label: The Virgin's head at the right end of the bed, eyes closed, her left hand hanging down

c2q.text: What thin line circles her head?

sources.title: Claudia Renzi, 'Caravaggio, la Morte della Vergine e una cortigiana da lui amata', About Art Online, 2025 (our translations)

c2a.text: Look again: too even and too fine for hair.

correction.tempting: Her long hair lies loose around her head.
correction.truth: The fine ring around her head is a thin gold halo.
correction.evidence: Look at the crop. Renzi (2025) describes the gold thread of the halo around her head.

c2b.text: Yes: one thin gold halo, easy to miss. Renzi calls it a thread of gold. No angels, no clouds lift her up.

c2c.text: Too fine for pearls: look again.

correction.tempting: The line is very thin and catches the light.
correction.truth: It is a thin gold halo, around her head.
correction.evidence: Look at the crop. Renzi (2025) describes the gold thread of the halo around her head.

c2m.text: One thin halo, nothing more. For the replacement, the friars wanted angels.

zoom.label: The left end of the bed, below the hem of the Virgin's red dress

c3.text: Level one: early writers gave reasons for the removal. Now zoom to the left end of the bed, below her red dress.

zoom.label: The left end of the bed, below the hem of the Virgin's red dress

c3q.text: What did Baglione complain of in 1642?

sources.title: Giovanni Baglione, Le vite de' pittori scultori et architetti (Rome, 1642), p. 138 (our translation)
Claudia Renzi, 'Caravaggio, la Morte della Vergine e una cortigiana da lui amata', About Art Online, 2025 (our translations)

c3a.text: She has one, just a very thin one.

correction.tempting: Her halo is hard to see.
correction.truth: Baglione wrote of a swollen Madonna with bare legs, painted with little decorum.
correction.evidence: Baglione, Lives (1642), p. 138; Renzi (2025) quotes the same passage.

c3b.text: There are no angels in this picture.

correction.truth: Here there are none; Baglione wrote of a swollen Madonna with bare legs.
correction.evidence: Baglione, Lives (1642), p. 138; Renzi (2025) quotes the same passage.

c3c.text: Yes. Baglione wrote that the Madonna was painted with little decorum, swollen and with bare legs (our translation).

c3m.text: Swollen, with bare legs: Baglione's words, printed in 1642. Whether that was the real reason is still argued.

extends.concept: From 'look for the basin' at the end of the level to what two scholars read in it: the washing of the dead body

c1q.what_you_learn: Renzi and Christiansen both connect the copper basin on the floor with washing the dead body; it is their reading, not a stated intention of Caravaggio's.

c1q.confidence: Medium-high: two independent scholars read the basin the same way (ledger virgin-029); no seventeenth-century text we read mentions the basin, so the answer is framed as the scholars' reading.
c1q.notes: Ledger virgin-029 (2+), virgin-004 (our looking: a shallow metal basin with a cloth over its rim), virgin-077 (barefoot friars, for the 'washing feet' near miss). Never stated as Caravaggio's intention.

extends.concept: From 'this is the Virgin Mary' and the friars' wish for angels (level) to the one sign of holiness Caravaggio did paint: a hair-thin halo

c2q.what_you_learn: The only sign of holiness around the dead Virgin is a very thin gold halo; there are no angels or clouds.

extends.concept: From the early writers' reasons (level) to the exact place in the picture Baglione's complaint points at: her bare legs

c3q.what_you_learn: Baglione (1642) wrote that the picture was taken away because the Madonna was painted with little decorum, swollen and with bare legs; the bare legs are at the left end of the bed.
